statement.informal: The improper Gaussian integral ∫₀^∞ exp(-t²) dt equals √π/2 -- proven from scratch in MachLib's Mathlib-free real-analysis base, zero new axioms. Built via a Laplace/Feynman parameter-differentiation trick: F(t) := gaussianI(t)², G(t) := ∫₀¹ exp(-t²(1+x²))/(1+x²) dx, F' = -G' via a from-scratch Leibniz differentiation-under-the-integral-sign theorem, hence F+G is constant on [0,∞), hence gaussianImproperIntegral² = F(0)+G(0) = 0 + π/4. π enters ONLY as a bare trig fact (cos(π/2)=0 / sin(π/2)=1) -- atan(1)=π/4 is DERIVED, not axiomatized, via a double application of the FTC to the same trivial integral. This is the normalizing constant behind the standard-normal density and, downstream, every Gaussian-noise estimation result (see structural_siblings).

common_mistakes.why_fails: Correct and fully proved as a standalone result (GaussianDiskSandwich.lean), but its OWN derivative in R doesn't close without genuine 2D polar coordinates (Jacobian r dr dθ) -- a 1D-only real-analysis base has no such machinery. Abandoned as the critical path after paper analysis, not because anything about it was wrong -- see forge_mined convention above: documenting a correct-but-stranded route is deliberate, not an omission.

Would make the whole theorem an elaborate restatement of the assumption -- pi never gets to 'meet' the integral through any real argument. Derived instead via two applications of ftc_riemann to the same trivial integral, using only pre-existing bare trig facts (cos(pi/2)=0, sin(pi/2)=1).
